claim: Predictions based on learned statistical regularities in the visual world facilitate attention and goal-directed behavior by sharpening the sensory representation of goal-relevant stimuli in advance.
source: Predictions based on learned statistical regularities in the visual world have been shown to facilitate attention and goal-directed behavior by sharpening the sensory representation of goal-relevant stimuli in advance.
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior research in the field, as indicated by the statement 'have been shown'.

claim: Expected distractor features could be decoded pre-stimulus from EEG signals.
source: We find that expected distractor features could not only be decoded pre-stimulus, but their representation differed from the representation of that same feature when part of the target.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the EEG decoding analysis presented in the study.

claim: The neural representation of expected distractor features differs from the representation of the same feature when it is part of the target.
source: We find that expected distractor features could not only be decoded pre-stimulus, but their representation differed from the representation of that same feature when part of the target.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-class decoding analysis showing distinct neural patterns for target versus distractor features.

claim: Spatial distractor expectations did not induce changes in preparatory neural activity.
source: Spatial distractor expectations did not induce changes in preparatory neural activity, but a strongly reduced Pd, an ERP index of inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-frequency analysis of pre-stimulus alpha-band activity showing no significant modulation.

claim: Spatial distractor expectations resulted in a strongly reduced Pd, an ERP index of inhibition.
source: Spatial distractor expectations did not induce changes in preparatory neural activity, but a strongly reduced Pd, an ERP index of inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis showing reduced Pd amplitude at high-probability distractor locations.

claim: Neural effects of statistical learning critically depend on the task relevance and dimension (spatial, feature) of predictions.
source: These results demonstrate that neural effects of statistical learning critically depend on the task relevance and dimension (spatial, feature) of predictions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential neural effects observed across conditions with varying spatial and feature predictability.

claim: Distractor suppression is not under voluntary top-down control.
source: Recent studies suggest that while attention can be flexibly directed at goal-relevant information, suppression of distracting information is not under similar voluntary top-down control (Chelazzi et al., 2019; Noonan et al., 2018), as was previously generally assumed (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies in the field.

claim: Distractor suppression strongly depends on distractor-based learning about its likely location in the visual environment.
source: Rather, this work shows that distractor suppression strongly depends on distractor-based learning, for example, about its likely location in the visual environment (Failing et al., 2019a; Ferrante et al., 2018; Goschy et al., 2014; Reder et al., 2003; Sauter et al., 2018; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a) or its non-spatial features, for example its color or shape (Cunningham and Egeth, 2016; Stilwell et al., 2019; Vatterott and Vecera, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Distractor suppression strongly depends on distractor-based learning about its non-spatial features such as color or shape.
source: Rather, this work shows that distractor suppression strongly depends on distractor-based learning, for example, about its likely location in the visual environment (Failing et al., 2019a; Ferrante et al., 2018; Goschy et al., 2014; Reder et al., 2003; Sauter et al., 2018; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a) or its non-spatial features, for example its color or shape (Cunningham and Egeth, 2016; Stilwell et al., 2019; Vatterott and Vecera, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Distractor inhibition may be dependent on expectations derived from past experience about the likelihood of events.
source: Based on these observations, it has been proposed that distractor inhibition may be dependent on expectations derived from past experience about the likelihood of events (Noonan et al., 2018; Moorselaar and Slagter, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical proposals in the field.

claim: In predictive processing frameworks, the brain continuously uses statistical regularities in the environment to predict the outside world with the overall aim of reducing the mismatch between its a priori predictions and the sensory input.
source: This idea is grounded in recent notions of predictive processing (Friston, 2009) in which the brain continuously uses statistical regularities in the environment to predict the outside world with the overall aim of reducing the mismatch between its a priori predictions and the sensory input.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to predictive processing theory.

claim: Processing of any expected stimulus, whether relevant or irrelevant, is reduced as it elicits a smaller prediction error.
source: In this framework, processing of any expected stimulus, whether relevant or irrelevant, is reduced (as it elicits a smaller prediction error).
evidence: This claim is based on the predictive processing framework described in the text.

claim: Distractor expectations should reduce subsequent distractor processing and interference.
source: Distractor expectations should hence reduce subsequent distractor processing and interference.
evidence: This claim is a logical inference from the predictive processing framework.

claim: It remains unclear how learned inhibition is neurally implemented.
source: Yet, it remains unclear how learned inhibition, which often occurs implicitly (Ferrante et al., 2018; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a), is neurally implemented.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in current knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Learned inhibition often occurs implicitly.
source: Yet, it remains unclear how learned inhibition, which often occurs implicitly (Ferrante et al., 2018; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a), is neurally implemented.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attention can bias sensory processing of expected task-relevant information in advance based on non-spatial feature information.
source: Many studies have shown that attention can bias sensory processing of expected task-relevant (or target) information in advance, both on the basis of non-spatial feature (Battistoni et al., 2017) and location information (Giesbrecht et al., 2006; Hopfinger et al., 2000; Kok et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attention can bias sensory processing of expected task-relevant information in advance based on location information.
source: Many studies have shown that attention can bias sensory processing of expected task-relevant (or target) information in advance, both on the basis of non-spatial feature (Battistoni et al., 2017) and location information (Giesbrecht et al., 2006; Hopfinger et al., 2000; Kok et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is unclear if expectations about upcoming distracting information can prepare the system in advance by modifying activity in sensory regions representing the expected distractor location or its non-spatial features.
source: Yet, it is currently unclear if expectations about upcoming distracting information can similarly prepare the system in advance by modifying activity in sensory regions representing the expected distractor location or its non-spatial features, or alternatively, that distractor learning only becomes apparent upon integration with incoming sensory information (Moorselaar and Slagter, 2020).
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: One EEG study reported increased pre-stimulus alpha-band activity over visual regions representing the likely distractor location, interpreted as top-down preparatory inhibition.
source: One recent EEG study reported increased pre-stimulus alpha-band activity over visual regions representing the likely distractor location, which was interpreted to reflect top-down preparatory inhibition (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Two EEG studies did not observe any learning-induced changes in preparatory activity of visual regions representing the expected distractor location.
source: In contrast, two other recent EEG studies did not observe any learning-induced changes in preparatory activity of visual regions representing the expected distractor location, as captured by pre-stimulus alpha-band activity (Noonan et al., 2016) or by changes in anticipatory spatial tuning as revealed by inverted encoding modeling based on alpha-band activity (van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: The discrepancy in findings about pre-stimulus alpha-band activity may be explained by differences in whether distractor features were fixed or varied across trials.
source: This discrepancy in findings may be explained by the fact that in the former study by Wang et al., 2019 distractor learning could only be location-based, as the shape and color of the distractor stimulus varied from trial to trial, while in the latter two studies distractor features were fixed, also permitting build-up of feature-based expectations.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on comparing different study designs.

claim: In the Wang et al., 2019 study, targets occurring at the likely distractor location were inhibited, as reflected by slower response times.
source: Indeed, in this study, it was also found that even targets occurring at the likely distractor location were inhibited, as reflected by slower response times.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific finding.

claim: When targets and distractors are assigned unique and fixed features, the suppression at high-probability distractor locations becomes specific to distractors.
source: Behavioral studies have also shown, however, that when targets and distractors are assigned unique and fixed features, the suppression at high-probability distractor locations becomes specific to distractors (Allenmark et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019), indicative of feature-based inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: The locus of distractor learning in the processing hierarchy is flexible and depends on the extent to which expectations are location- and/or feature-specific.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the locus of distractor learning in the processing hierarchy is flexible and depends on the extent to which expectations are location- and/or feature-specific.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the cited behavioral studies.

claim: There is no neural evidence for feature-based distractor templates that set up the system in advance to inhibit distractor processing.
source: Although some behavioral findings are in line with this idea (Arita et al., 2012; Carlisle and Nitka, 2018; Park et al., 2007; Woodman and Luck, 2007), to date there is no neural evidence for feature-based distractor templates that set up the system in advance to inhibit distractor processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: Previous studies that investigated distractor templates cued the distractor on a trial-by-trial basis, preventing distractor learning.
source: However, the few studies that investigated this, cued the distractor on a trial-by-trial basis (de Vries et al., 2019; Reeder et al., 2018), preventing distractor learning and leaving open the possibility that anticipatory distractor feature templates only arise after repeated encounters with the to-be-ignored feature, that is when statistical learning is possible.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies and identifies a methodological limitation.

claim: Anticipatory distractor feature templates may only arise after repeated encounters with the to-be-ignored feature when statistical learning is possible.
source: However, the few studies that investigated this, cued the distractor on a trial-by-trial basis (de Vries et al., 2019; Reeder et al., 2018), preventing distractor learning and leaving open the possibility that anticipatory distractor feature templates only arise after repeated encounters with the to-be-ignored feature, that is when statistical learning is possible.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about when distractor templates might arise.

claim: In Experiment 1, 18 participants performed a visual search task.
source: To this end, observers (N = 18) performed a visual search task in which the distractor and the target either had the same spatial frequency and only differed in orientation (referred to as Distractor predictable Target predictable [DpTp] identical condition), or differed both in spatial frequency and orientation.
evidence: This claim is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 1, in feature specific search (DpTp unique), spatial benefits were smaller than during feature non-specific searches.
source: Specifically, in feature specific search (i.e. DpTp unique) spatial benefits were smaller than during feature non-specific searches (DpTp unique vs. DpTp identical, t (17)=3.0, p=0.008, d = 0.71; DpTp unique vs. DvTv unique, t (17)=2.0, p=0.06, d = 0.48; BF10 = 1.3), whereas spatial benefits did not differ between the two feature non-specific search conditions (DpTp identical vs. DvTv unique, t (17)=1.3, p=0.22, d = 0.30; BF01 = 2.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by planned comparisons with statistical tests.

claim: In Experiment 1, the findings are indicative of stronger suppression at the high-probability distractor location in the condition in which expectations could necessarily only develop at the spatial level.
source: These findings are indicative of stronger suppression at the high-probability distractor location in the condition in which expectations could necessarily only develop at the spatial level.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: In Experiment 1, after excluding trials where distractor location repeated, distractors were still more efficiently ignored on high-probability distractor locations across all conditions.
source: Importantly, however, across all conditions distractors were more efficiently ignored on high-probability distractor locations (all t's > 2.6, all p's < 0.018, all d's > 0.62) demonstrating that intertrial location priming could not entirely account for the observed reduction in distractor interference at the high-probability distractor location, as also reported in previous studies (e.g. Failing et al., 2019b; Ferrante et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by control analysis excluding priming effects.

claim: In Experiment 1, intertrial location priming could not entirely account for the observed reduction in distractor interference at the high-probability distractor location.
source: Importantly, however, across all conditions distractors were more efficiently ignored on high-probability distractor locations (all t's > 2.6, all p's < 0.018, all d's > 0.62) demonstrating that intertrial location priming could not entirely account for the observed reduction in distractor interference at the high-probability distractor location, as also reported in previous studies (e.g. Failing et al., 2019b; Ferrante et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by control analysis and citations to prior research.

claim: In Experiment 1, distractor interference is most reduced when distractors can be predicted at both the spatial and feature level.
source: To summarize, Experiment 1 showed that (1) distractor interference is most reduced when distractors can be predicted at both the spatial and feature level; (1) distractor location learning is more pronounced when distractors can only be predicted on the basis of location, but not feature information; and that (3) any stimulus presented at the expected distractor location is automatically inhibited, including targets.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, distractor location learning is more pronounced when distractors can only be predicted on the basis of location, but not feature information.
source: To summarize, Experiment 1 showed that (1) distractor interference is most reduced when distractors can be predicted at both the spatial and feature level; (1) distractor location learning is more pronounced when distractors can only be predicted on the basis of location, but not feature information; and that (3) any stimulus presented at the expected distractor location is automatically inhibited, including targets.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, any stimulus presented at the expected distractor location is automatically inhibited, including targets.
source: To summarize, Experiment 1 showed that (1) distractor interference is most reduced when distractors can be predicted at both the spatial and feature level; (1) distractor location learning is more pronounced when distractors can only be predicted on the basis of location, but not feature information; and that (3) any stimulus presented at the expected distractor location is automatically inhibited, including targets.
evidence: This claim summarizes the findings from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, 24 participants performed a visual search task while EEG was recorded.
source: The goal of Experiment 2 (N = 24) was threefold.
evidence: This claim is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, the benefit of distractor location predictability was most pronounced when distractors and targets consistently shared the same spatial frequency and learning could only be location-based.
source: Indeed, the benefit of distractor location predictability (i.e. high vs. low) was most pronounced when distractors and targets consistently shared the same spatial frequency and learning could only be location-based (M = 50.9 ± SD=24.4; DpTp identical vs. DpTp unique: t (23)=4.6, p<0.001, d = 0.93; DpTp identical vs. DpTv unique; t (23)=4.1, p<0.001, d = 0.84), intermediate when feature prediction could be formulated only for the distractor (M = 41.7 ± SD=20.1) and smallest when feature predictions could be formulated for both the distractor and target (M = 30.6 ± SD=10.7; DpTv unique vs. DpTp unique: t (23)=3.0, p=0.005, d = 0.62).
evidence: This claim is supported by planned comparisons with statistical tests.

claim: In Experiment 2, distractor feature learning may shift the locus in the visual hierarchy at which expectation-based suppression operates from space-based to feature-based.
source: These results suggest that distractor feature learning may shift the locus in the visual hierarchy at which expectation-based suppression operates from space-based to feature-based.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: The visual system continues to be sensitive to feature information at a location that is suppressed in advance.
source: Together, these results replicate the finding of Experiment one that the visual system continues to be sensitive to feature information at a location that is suppressed in advance (Stilwell et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data and citation to prior research.

claim: Target processing was impaired to the same extent across conditions, arguing for a fixed level of suppression tied to the high-probability location.
source: Whereas target processing was impaired to the same extent across conditions, arguing for a fixed level of suppression tied to the high-probability location, subsequent inhibition of distracting stimuli at this location was modulated by expectations at the feature level, with suppression being most pronounced when learning could necessarily only be space-based.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: Subsequent inhibition of distracting stimuli at the high-probability location was modulated by expectations at the feature level, with suppression being most pronounced when learning could necessarily only be space-based.
source: Whereas target processing was impaired to the same extent across conditions, arguing for a fixed level of suppression tied to the high-probability location, subsequent inhibition of distracting stimuli at this location was modulated by expectations at the feature level, with suppression being most pronounced when learning could necessarily only be space-based.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: When expectations can be grounded in longer learning, the system combines spatial and feature information about probable upcoming distractors to reduce distractor interference.
source: In Experiment 2, this interaction between spatial and feature expectations remained significant even after controlling for spatial intertrial transitions, suggesting that when expectations can be grounded in longer learning, the system combines spatial and feature information about probable upcoming distractors to reduce distractor interference.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: Cluster-based permutation tests did not show any reliable increase of alpha-power contralateral vs. ipsilateral to the high-probability distractor location in any condition.
source: As visualized in Figure 3A/B, cluster-based permutation tests across time and frequency and across time for lateralization index averaged within the alpha-band (8–12 Hz) did not show any reliable increase of alpha-power contralateral vs. ipsilateral to the high-probability distractor location in any condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 3.

claim: The observed spatial suppression at the high-probability distractor location at the behavioral level was not mediated by a contralateral increase of alpha-band power in anticipation of search display onset.
source: Thus, these time-frequency findings suggest that the observed spatial suppression at the high-probability distractor location at the behavioral level was not mediated by a contralateral increase of alpha-band power in anticipation of search display onset, even in a condition in which learning could only occur at the spatial level and across a longer time span than in two previous studies that also did not observe distractor learning-related changes in pre-stimulus alpha-band activity (Noonan et al., 2016; van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2019), but in contrast to another study (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the time-frequency analysis results, with citations to prior research.

claim: The classifier could discriminate not only the target, but also the distractor's spatial frequency, in all conditions.
source: Classification performance visualized in Figure 4 shows that the classifier could discriminate not only the target, but also the distractor's spatial frequency, in all conditions(as it is unclear whether in the DpTp identical condition, in which targets and distractors were of the same spatial frequency, classification was driven by the spatial frequency of the target, of the distractor or both, we did not contrast this condition with the unique feature conditions).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Target decoding was numerically higher when its spatial frequency was predictable compared to when it was not.
source: Interestingly, both in anticipation and during stimulus processing, target decoding was numerically higher when its spatial frequency was predictable (i.e. DpTp unique condition) compared to when it was not (i.e. DpTv unique condition), whereas the opposite pattern was observed for distractor decoding: the spatial frequency of the distractor could be decoded with higher accuracy when only the spatial frequency of the distractor, but not the target spatial frequency could be predicted in advance (in the DpTv unique compared to the DpTp unique condition).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of decoding performance patterns.

claim: The spatial frequency of the distractor could be decoded with higher accuracy when only the spatial frequency of the distractor, but not the target spatial frequency could be predicted in advance.
source: Interestingly, both in anticipation and during stimulus processing, target decoding was numerically higher when its spatial frequency was predictable (i.e. DpTp unique condition) compared to when it was not (i.e. DpTv unique condition), whereas the opposite pattern was observed for distractor decoding: the spatial frequency of the distractor could be decoded with higher accuracy when only the spatial frequency of the distractor, but not the target spatial frequency could be predicted in advance (in the DpTv unique compared to the DpTp unique condition).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of decoding performance patterns.

claim: Anticipatory target decoding was absent in the DpTv unique condition, the one condition where target expectations could not develop.
source: Critically, anticipatory target decoding was absent in the DpTv unique condition, the one condition where target expectations could not develop, arguing against the possibility that the observed anticipatory decoding can be explained by an artificial shift of the stimulus-evoked response (van Driel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis results and argues against an alternative explanation.

claim: Anticipatory above chance decoding only emerged close to search display onset.
source: Also note that anticipatory above chance decoding was not sustained throughout the entire pre-stimulus period, but only emerged close to search display onset, raising the possibility suggesting that sustained anticipatory expectation signals were subtracted out by the baselining procedure (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of the temporal pattern of decoding performance.

claim: Anticipatory target decoding was specific to the DpTp unique condition.
source: As visualized by the red and green colored horizontal lines in Figure 4A (p<0.05, cluster-corrected), anticipatory target decoding was specific to the DpTp unique condition, whereas anticipatory distractor decoding was specific to the DpTv unique condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation tests shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Anticipatory distractor decoding was specific to the DpTv unique condition.
source: As visualized by the red and green colored horizontal lines in Figure 4A (p<0.05, cluster-corrected), anticipatory target decoding was specific to the DpTp unique condition, whereas anticipatory distractor decoding was specific to the DpTv unique condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation tests shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When both the targets and the distractors spatial frequency could be predicted, participants especially relied on target feature-specific information to guide search.
source: These statistical results reveal that when both the targets and the distractors spatial frequency could be predicted, participants especially relied on target feature-specific information to guide search.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the decoding analysis results.

claim: When participants could not know what the target would look like, they relied more on distractor feature-specific information to bias search, already in anticipation of search display onset.
source: However, when they could not know what the target would look like, as it randomly varied across trials, and the target should thus also not be evident in the anticipatory neural code, participants relied more on distractor feature-specific information to bias search, and importantly, already in anticipation of search display onset.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the decoding analysis results.

claim: Target decoding was better in the DpTp unique than in the DpTv unique condition both before and after target presentation.
source: These interactions reflected better target decoding in the DpTp unique than in the DpTv unique condition both before and after target presentation (t (23)=2.1, p=0.044, d = 0.44 and t (23)=4.0, p<0.001, d = 0.82, respectively) and vice versa for distractor decoding (t (23)=2.1, p=0.046, d = 0.43 and t (23)=2.5, p=0.02, d = 0.51, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by follow-up statistical tests.

claim: Distractor decoding was better in the DpTv unique than in the DpTp unique condition both before and after distractor presentation.
source: These interactions reflected better target decoding in the DpTp unique than in the DpTv unique condition both before and after target presentation (t (23)=2.1, p=0.044, d = 0.44 and t (23)=4.0, p<0.001, d = 0.82, respectively) and vice versa for distractor decoding (t (23)=2.1, p=0.046, d = 0.43 and t (23)=2.5, p=0.02, d = 0.51, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by follow-up statistical tests.

claim: We could decode the spatial frequency of the target from the pattern of pre-search display brain activity.
source: Together, these findings show that we could not only decode the spatial frequency of the target from the pattern of pre-search display brain activity, but also, when the targets spatial frequency was unpredictable, the spatial frequency of the distractor, suggestive of a distractor feature template.
evidence: This claim summarizes the decoding analysis results.

claim: When the targets spatial frequency was unpredictable, we could decode the spatial frequency of the distractor from pre-search display brain activity, suggestive of a distractor feature template.
source: Together, these findings show that we could not only decode the spatial frequency of the target from the pattern of pre-search display brain activity, but also, when the targets spatial frequency was unpredictable, the spatial frequency of the distractor, suggestive of a distractor feature template.
evidence: This claim summarizes the decoding analysis results and provides an interpretation.

claim: A hallmark of an advance rejection template is that processing of the coded features is inhibited and the neural representation of a rejection template should be distinct from a target-defined attentional template.
source: A hallmark of an advance rejection template is that processing of the coded features is inhibited and the neural representation of a rejection template should thus be distinct from a target-defined attentional template which in contrast facilitates processing of matching stimuli.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical reasoning about rejection templates.

claim: The predictable target spatial frequency could only be decoded from the pattern of pre-stimulus EEG activity using target-based classification weights, but not using distractor-based classification weights.
source: Indeed, using distractor trained weights, the exact same spatial frequency could no longer be decoded above change in advance when it was a predictable feature of the target, potentially indicative of a distinct distractor template (Figure 5A; dashed lines). That is, the predictable target spatial frequency could only be decoded from the pattern of pre-stimulus EEG activity using target-based classification weights, but not using distractor-based classification weights, even though this same spatial frequency could be reconstructed using distractor-based decoding (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-class decoding analysis results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Pre-stimulus target decoding performance of the distractor-trained model did not differ between the conditions in which the target spatial frequency could be predicted in advance vs. could not be predicted in advance.
source: What's more, pre-stimulus target decoding performance of the distractor-trained model did not differ between the conditions in which the target spatial frequency could be predicted in advance vs. could not be predicted in advance, neither when tested with cluster correction nor with paired t-tests within the pre-search display window (t (23)=0.57, p=0.57, d = 0.12; BF01 = 4.03) or the post-search display window (t (23)=0.14, p=0.89, d = 0.028; BF01 = 4.61).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical tests on cross-class decoding performance.

claim: Cluster-based permutation tests identified significant below chance decoding during visual search using the distractor trained weights.
source: Next to these anticipatory effects, cluster-based permutation tests identified significant below chance decoding during visual search using the distractor trained weights (p<0.05, cluster-corrected; dashed green horizontal lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster-based permutation tests shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Spatial frequency was differently represented in the pattern of scalp EEG activity as a function of whether it was a feature of the target or of the distractor.
source: Together, these findings suggest that spatial frequency was differently represented in the pattern of scalp EEG activity as a function of whether it was a feature of the target or of the distractor.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the cross-class decoding results.

claim: A clear distractor-evoked N2pc was observed in all conditions.
source: As visualized in Figure 6, we observed a clear distractor-evoked N2pc in all conditions, which only seemed to be somewhat reduced in amplitude at the high-probability distractor location in the DpTp unique condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The target-evoked N2pc appeared to be virtually unaffected by feature and/or location expectations.
source: Likewise, as shown in Figure 7, the target-evoked N2pc also appeared to be virtually unaffected by feature and/or location expectations.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The distractor-evoked Pd was virtually eliminated when distractors appeared at high-probability distractor locations.
source: Yet, notably, and in line with our previous study (van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2019), the distractor-evoked Pd was virtually eliminated when distractors appeared at high-probability distractor locations, signaling a reduced need for post-distractor inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis results and citation to prior research.

claim: Distractors continued to capture attention to the same extent at high as at low-probability distractor locations.
source: The N2pc results suggest that distractors continued to capture attention to the same extent at high as at low-probability distractor locations, albeit generally not as strongly as targets.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the N2pc results.

claim: At high-probability locations there appeared to be a reduced need to actively counteract the shift of attention as evidenced by a reduction in the amplitude of the distractor-evoked Pd.
source: Yet, at high-probability locations there appeared to be a reduced need to actively counteract this shift of attention as evidenced by a reduction in the amplitude of the distractor-evoked Pd.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the Pd results.

claim: In a context that enforced learning at the spatial level, distractors at expected locations continued to elicit an N2pc, but the subsequent Pd was virtually eliminated.
source: Intriguingly, we recently found that in a context that enforced learning at the spatial level, as distractors and targets were very similar at the feature level (i.e. same spatial frequency), distractors at expected locations continued to elicit an N2pc, but the subsequent Pd was virtually eliminated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: There was no more need for post-distractor inhibition once participants had learned that information at a specific location could be safely ignored.
source: We interpreted this as if there was no more need for post-distractor inhibition once participants had learned that information at a specific location could be safely ignored (van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2019).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation from prior research by the authors.

claim: Expectations about features of upcoming distractors in the environment induce pre-stimulus sensory templates.
source: In brief, our results demonstrate that expectations about features of upcoming distractors in the environment induce pre-stimulus sensory templates.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Pre-stimulus sensory templates differed as a function of whether the feature was a predictable feature of the target or of the distractor, providing evidence for distinct target and distractor templates.
source: Crucially, these sensory templates differed as a function of whether the feature was a predictable feature of the target or of the distractor, providing evidence for distinct target and distractor templates.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: There is no evidence for a preparatory spatial bias as a function of distractor location predictability, as no modulations of pre-stimulus alpha-band activity were observed.
source: Yet, we find no evidence for a preparatory spatial bias as a function of distractor location predictability, as no modulations of pre-stimulus alpha-band activity were observed.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Distractors at expected locations evoked a smaller Pd, indicative of a reduced need for inhibition, independent of distractor feature expectations.
source: Distractors at expected locations did evoke a smaller Pd, indicative of a reduced need for inhibition, independent of distractor feature expectations.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Neural effects of predictions based on regularities in the environment critically depend not only on the task relevance (target, distractor), but also the dimension (spatial, feature) of these regularities.
source: Thus, neural effects of predictions based on regularities in the environment critically depend not only on the task relevance (target, distractor), but also the dimension (spatial, feature) of these regularities.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main conclusions of the study.

claim: Previously observed modulations of pre-stimulus alpha-band activity may reflect attending away rather than suppression of distracting information.
source: Previously observed modulations of pre-stimulus alpha-band activity may instead reflect attending away rather than suppression of distracting information, as also argued previously (Foster and Awh, 2019).
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the interpretation of prior findings, supported by citation.

claim: Target facilitation and distractor suppression rely on distinct neural mechanisms, at least when space-based.
source: Together, these findings suggest that target facilitation and distractor suppression rely on distinct neural mechanisms, at least when space-based.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the current and prior findings.

claim: Distractor location learning may be implemented via an activity silent mechanism or synaptic efficiency.
source: Albeit speculative, distractor location learning may be implemented via an activity silent mechanism or synaptic efficiency (Stokes, 2015).
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the neural mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: Distractor learning may change plasticity in priority maps of space.
source: An intuitively appealing idea, one that can also be easily reconciled with proposals that (spatial) expectations exert their influence only after initial processing of sensory input (Alilović et al., 2019; Rao et al., 2012), is that distractor learning changes plasticity in priority maps of space (Ferrante et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the neural mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: A distinct distractor template may only arise as a function of learning from repeated encounters with the to-be-ignored feature.
source: Counter to these previous studies, which cued the distractor feature on a trial-by-trial basis, hence promoting the use of visual working memory, here the distractor 'template' could be formed on the basis of predictions derived from regularities in the search context. That we could decode the predictable distractor feature under these conditions thus suggests that a distinct distractor template may only arise as a function of learning from repeated encounters with the to-be-ignored feature.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the decoding results.

claim: The development of distractor templates may rely on implicit learning mechanisms that bypass working memory altogether.
source: The development of this template may rely on implicit learning mechanisms that bypass working memory altogether (Moorselaar and Slagter, 2020) and hence should not be taken as evidence for the existence of templates for rejection in working memory.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the mechanism underlying distractor templates, supported by citation.

claim: Distractor feature expectations induce pre-stimulus sensory templates.
source: Nevertheless, they do convincingly show that distractor feature expectations, like target feature expectations, induce pre-stimulus sensory templates.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the decoding results.

claim: The visual system can strategically boost features shifted away from the distractor and/or target to increase discriminability between the target and the likely distractors.
source: Indeed, it is well known that the visual system can strategically boost features shifted away from the distractor and/or target to increase discriminability between the target and the likely distractors (Geng and Witkowski, 2019; Navalpakkam and Itti, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: While we could decode the anticipated spatial frequency of the target above chance in target-only trials prior to search display onset when the model was trained on target spatial frequencies, we could not decode the same anticipated spatial frequency of the target when the model was trained on distractor spatial frequencies.
source: Strikingly, we found that while we could decode the anticipated spatial frequency of the target above chance in target-only trials prior to search display onset when the model was trained on target spatial frequencies, we could not decode the same anticipated spatial frequency of the target when the model was trained on distractor spatial frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-class decoding analysis results.

claim: After search display onset there was reliable below-chance decoding in cross-class analysis, which arose because after search display onset, attention was shifted to the target spatial frequency during training on the distractor spatial frequency.
source: What's more, after search display onset there was reliable below-chance decoding, which arguably arose because after search display onset, attention was shifted to the target spatial frequency during training on the distractor spatial frequency, resulting in negative decoding when the classifier was tested on the target-only trials and the target now possessed the distractor spatial frequency.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the cross-class decoding results.

claim: The cross-class decoding results argue against the idea that attention was strategically shifted away toward one (or both) of the remaining (and possible target) spatial frequencies.
source: Although these are exploratory null findings and therefore should be interpreted cautiously, they nevertheless argue against the idea that attention was strategically shifted away toward one (or both) of the remaining (and possible target) spatial frequencies, but rather support the notion of a distinct distractor template.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the cross-class decoding results.

claim: It is unlikely that the observed anticipatory distractor feature decoding simply reflects inter-trial priming.
source: Note also that it is unlikely that the observed anticipatory distractor feature decoding simply reflects inter-trial priming as in this scenario, one would not expect a difference in the neural activity patterns driving distractor decoding versus target decoding, as was observed here.
evidence: This claim is an inference that argues against an alternative explanation.

claim: Target and distractor feature expectations are implemented in distinct neural codes.
source: Together, these decoding results indicate that target and distractor feature expectations are implemented in distinct neural codes.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the cross-class decoding results.

claim: The Pd signals a suppressive mechanism, which is stronger in contexts that require strong suppression.
source: Following the idea that the Pd signals a suppressive mechanism, which is stronger in contexts that require strong suppression (Hickey et al., 2009), these findings are typically interpreted to reflect the suppression of salient distractors before they capture attention (Gaspelin and Luck, 2018b).
evidence: This claim is based on citations to prior research and theoretical interpretations.

claim: It is unclear why in certain contexts the Pd increases, whereas in others its amplitude decreases as a function of expectations.
source: To date, it is unclear why in certain contexts the Pd increases, whereas in others, as in the current study, its amplitudes decreases as a function of expectations (Heuer and Schubö, 2020).
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in current knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: The N2pc and the Pd reflect different attentional mechanisms, as these components were differentially sensitive to feature and spatial expectations.
source: Our ERP findings also corroborate the notion that the N2pc and the Pd reflect different attentional mechanisms, as these components were differentially sensitive to feature and spatial expectations.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the ERP results.

claim: The N2pc indexes object individuation, the formation of an object representation that is segregated from the background and other items in the display.
source: Although it was initially thought that the N2pc reflects a covert shift of attention to a peripheral stimulus (Eimer, 1996; Woodman and Luck, 1999), current evidence suggests that the N2pc indexes object individuation (Mazza and Caramazza, 2015), the formation of an object representation that is segregated from the background and other items in the display (Kahneman et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The N2pc reflects attentional engagement, which reflects the deployment of higher level processes that enable identification and binding of stimulus features.
source: In one perspective, which is easily reconciled with the idea of object individuation, the N2pc reflects attentional engagement, which according to Zivony et al., 2018 reflects the deployment of higher level processes that enable identification and binding of stimulus features, and, if necessary, consolidation into working memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: When the spatial frequency of both the target and the distractor were predictable, and distractors and targets could thus easily be dissociated, the distractor-evoked N2pc was smaller in amplitude, whereas the target-evoked N2pc increased in amplitude.
source: Consistent with this perspective, here we show that when the spatial frequency of both the target and the distractor were predictable, and distractors and targets could thus easily be dissociated, the distractor-evoked N2pc was smaller in amplitude, whereas the target-evoked N2pc increased in amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis results.

claim: The Pd was only sensitive to spatial expectations in that its amplitude was greatly reduced to distractors at the high-probability distractor location.
source: By contrast, as outlined above, the Pd was only sensitive to spatial expectations in that its amplitude was greatly reduced to distractors at the high-probability distractor location.
evidence: This claim is supported by ERP analysis results.

claim: The Pd is often used to index stimulus-driven distractor inhibition.
source: This demonstrates that the Pd, which is often used to index stimulus-driven distractor inhibition (Gaspelin and Luck, 2018b; Sawaki et al., 2012), is specifically sensitive to learned expectations at the spatial level.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Distractor suppression at the high-probability distractor location, but not target suppression at the high-probability distractor location, was affected by stimulus feature regularities.
source: At the behavioral level, we found that distractor suppression at the high-probability distractor location, but not target suppression at the high-probability distractor location, was affected by stimulus feature regularities.
evidence: This claim summarizes the behavioral findings.

claim: Spatial distractor expectations may induce feature-blind 'proactive' suppression which uniformly suppresses both distractor and target processing at the expected distractor location.
source: This may suggest that while spatial distractor expectations may induce feature-blind 'proactive' suppression (which uniformly suppresses both distractor and target processing at the expected distractor location), subsequent inhibition of stimuli at the likely distractor location is dependent on expectations about what a distractor looks like at the feature level.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: Subsequent inhibition of stimuli at the likely distractor location is dependent on expectations about what a distractor looks like at the feature level.
source: This may suggest that while spatial distractor expectations may induce feature-blind 'proactive' suppression (which uniformly suppresses both distractor and target processing at the expected distractor location), subsequent inhibition of stimuli at the likely distractor location is dependent on expectations about what a distractor looks like at the feature level.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: The interaction between spatial and feature expectations in the distractor tuned behavioral analyses was significant in both Experiments 1 and 2.
source: While the interaction between spatial and feature expectations in the distractor tuned behavioral analyses was significant in both Experiments 1 and 2, after priming effects were removed, it only remained significant in Experiment 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: After priming effects were removed, the interaction between spatial and feature expectations only remained significant in Experiment 2.
source: While the interaction between spatial and feature expectations in the distractor tuned behavioral analyses was significant in both Experiments 1 and 2, after priming effects were removed, it only remained significant in Experiment 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The interaction between spatial and feature expectations may to some extent reflect an interaction between priming and distractor feature expectations.
source: This may suggest that the interaction also to some extent reflects an interaction between priming and distractor feature expectations, but could also reflect the fact that Experiment 2 allowed for the development of more robust feature and location expectations.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: Experiment 2 allowed for the development of more robust feature and location expectations compared to Experiment 1.
source: That is, counter to Experiment 2, in Experiment 1, conditions not only switched every block (and consequently also the predictable distractor and/or target features), but participants also only completed six blocks per condition. In Experiment 2, distractor location and feature learning could develop over a much longer time scale (18 blocks), and participants completed 36 blocks per condition. Consequently, Experiment 1 may have been less sensitive to detecting the interaction between feature and spatial expectations above and beyond intertrial priming.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on comparing the experimental designs.

claim: None of the EEG measures showed an interaction between spatial and feature expectations.
source: It may seem surprising at first that none of our EEG measures showed an interaction between spatial and feature expectations, while in the corresponding behavioral data, we found that distractor interference was most reduced when both the location and the spatial frequency of the distractor were predictable in advance.
evidence: This claim is based on the EEG analysis results.

claim: The EEG measures may be less sensitive to revealing neural mechanisms that integrate spatial and feature distractor foreknowledge.
source: Yet, this may be explained by the fact that these EEG measures are specifically tuned to capturing modulations in either spatial processing (i.e. spatially lateralized measures (alpha asymmetry and Pd)) or feature representation (spatial frequency decoding). As such, they may be less sensitive to revealing neural mechanisms that integrate spatial and feature distractor foreknowledge.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the limitations of the EEG measures.

claim: The EEG data showed robust main effects of spatial and feature expectations.
source: Indeed, our EEG data did show robust main effects of spatial and feature expectations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the EEG analysis results.

claim: Feature-based distractor expectations, but not location-based distractor expectations, modulate pre-stimulus representations.
source: They extend this work by showing that feature-based distractor expectations, but not location-based distractor expectations, modulate pre-stimulus representations, and in a distinct manner from expectations about upcoming target features, indicative of a distractor template.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Feature-based distractor expectations modulate pre-stimulus representations in a distinct manner from expectations about upcoming target features, indicative of a distractor template.
source: They extend this work by showing that feature-based distractor expectations, but not location-based distractor expectations, modulate pre-stimulus representations, and in a distinct manner from expectations about upcoming target features, indicative of a distractor template.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The findings have important implications for cognitive (neuroscience) theories of selective attention and predictive processing.
source: These findings have important implications for cognitive (neuroscience) theories of selective attention and predictive processing.
evidence: This claim is a statement about the broader significance of the findings.
